title: NBA League Pass Rankings: Part 4
contentHtml:
Welcome to Part 4 of our NBA League Pass Rankings here at The Lowe Post. Last week, we published the first three parts, covering teams 30 through 13. (Check out Part 1 for a refresher on our methodology.)

Today, the countdown continues with nos. 12 through 7. Tomorrow, we’ll finish up with the top six.

Reminder: We’ve rolled out these League Pass Rankings in separate installments as part of the lead-up to the new NBA season; next week, this newsletter will convert to its usual once-per-week cadence. Now back to the rankings:

Subscribe now

12. Toronto Raptors (34)

Recent weeks have brought welcome clarity:

  • Kawhi Leonard, having paid relatively little for contributing to the ruin of a franchise, is a Raptor—again.

  • Toronto’s revamped court is fantastic, even if it appears as if an unseen dinosaur has clawed the very essence of Canada (the maple leaf) in addition to his or her usual target (the basketball):

  • And most importantly: Jack Armstrong is back as an analyst, the Raptors’ new controlling owners having avoided a fumble worse than one of the many that Jack’s beloved Buffalo Bills have coughed up in the playoffs. (Sorry!)

The Raptors should be very good but a little grimy—even with Leonard’s shooting touch unclogging what had been a pretty jumbled half-court offense. Leonard is still one of the league’s marvels, with that old-school, leaning midranger, set up with a bevy of Fundamentally Sound shoulder shimmies and head fakes.

He can still amp up his defense to something like 90 percent peak Sharktopus Mode, spreading those impossible arms and fingers, pouncing from the weak side to swarm entry passes, and sometimes just straight up taking the ball from people like Jerry Seinfeld swiping the rye from that old battle-ax (or like Leonard once did twice in succession to Ben McLemore—the Kings, yet again—damn near ending the man’s career in 45 seconds).

Leonard accentuates everything the Raptors are already good at and boosts them in weaker areas: jump-shooting, defending without fouling, 3-point volume (assuming he takes as many as he did last season). Sadly, it is now impossible to fully enjoy Leonard—to watch him without thinking of all That Stuff.

Good freaking luck even approaching the rim when the Raptors have Leonard, Scottie Barnes, and Collin Murray-Boyles switching every action and poking at the ball with the relentlessness of hungry, hungry hippos. Toss in Jamal Shead, and the Raptors can build some of the league’s stingiest defensive lineups. They’ll force piles of turnovers and run like hell off of them. The watchability downside: lots of free throws, both ways.

Murray-Boyles is primed for more minutes, including as a small-ball center if Jakob Poeltl flounders. (Poeltl’s free throws make for good theater.) Immanuel Quickley is one of the league’s major swing factors. Kyle Anderson’s slowness will make defenders lunge at ghosts. Trayce Jackson-Davis can play—and dunk.

Don’t be surprised if Barnes is recognized as a top-10 player by season’s end.

The Raptor, like Benny the Bull and maybe one or two other mascots, merits his own broadcast feed.

Be careful what you wish for shoving RJ Barrett into every fake trade. He is not the ideal complementary player in some senses—including his salary—but he’s a chameleon who can do lots of things pretty well and showed no fear of big moments in last year’s playoffs.
